objective: Catch context-dependent design claims stated as universal rules.

sources.title: Liu et al. 2023, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
AWS: How content chunking works for knowledge bases

followUp.question: For each trade-off here, name the measurement that would settle it for a specific system.

transfer.scenario: A teammate proposes 2,000-token chunks and top-k of 25 'to be safe'. Respond as the design reviewer.
rubric: many chunks add noise cost latency
relevant info in middle can be under-used
tune with retrieval and answer metrics

narration.text: The client has a forty-page FAQ that changes once a year and is open to all staff.
For that FAQ, putting the whole thing in the prompt with caching is a reasonable option to test against RAG.
For the fifty-thousand-page policy library, we need retrieval.
We'll use large chunks, because each one carries more context for the model and that gives better answers.
We'll retrieve the top twenty chunks for every question, since more evidence gives the model more to work with.
Questions like 'what's the status of my ticket' should go to the ticketing system's API, not vector search.
We'll add a reranker, but only if tests show it improves results enough to justify the extra latency.

planted.whyWrong: Chunk size is a trade-off. Larger chunks keep surrounding context but dilute the similarity match and use more of the context window; smaller chunks match precisely but can lose meaning. The right size depends on the documents and is set by evaluation.
acceptableCorrections: Chunk size is a trade-off between context and precise matching; we tune it with retrieval tests.
Use structure-aware or hierarchical chunking, or attach headings, instead of just making chunks bigger.
planted.exceptions: For documents with long, tightly connected sections, larger chunks may well score better; the error is treating it as a general rule without testing.

explain: large: more context but diluted match and window cost

planted.misconception: More retrieved chunks can only help.
planted.whyWrong: Raising k increases the chance the answer is included, but adds irrelevant text, cost and latency, and models can under-use evidence buried in the middle of long inputs. k is tuned with recall and answer-quality metrics, often with a reranker to keep the best few.
acceptableCorrections: More chunks raise recall but add noise, cost and latency; we pick k from evaluation.
Retrieve more candidates, then rerank and keep the best few.
planted.exceptions: If recall at a small k is poor and latency budget allows, a larger k can be the right choice. Anthropic's 2024 contextual-retrieval post found top-20 beat top-10 and top-5 on its datasets and advised experimenting on your own use case. So twenty is not the error; the error is the reasoning that more evidence always helps, applied to every question without measuring noise, cost and latency.
